title: Why did the Chinese alternate zong and heng rods?
description: Forty one is written with zong rods only, and the five rods in a row are read in other ways when no clear space separates the places. The check shows that alternating zong and heng keeps neighbouring places apart.
teaching_notes: One idea: a row of identical rods has no visible break between places, so changing the shape marks where one place ends. Watch for students who think the five rods can only mean forty one.

video_script.why: The child uses the idea from the Mesopotamian example that unclear gaps allow two readings, and finds the other readings of five identical rods to see why the Chinese alternated zong and heng.
video_script.substitution: The unclear gap is now between identical rods in neighbouring places, so the five rods can be split in several ways.
video_script.anchor: the book's Chinese rod numerals: zong and heng shapes taking turns from the ones place
video_script.payoff_line: Alternating shapes keep neighbouring places apart, so forty one cannot be misread.

final_answer.value: To keep neighbouring places apart; with zongs only 41 is 4 rods and 1 rod, which could also be read as 5, 23, 32 or 122
final_answer.spoken: To keep neighbouring places apart; with zongs only forty one is four rods and one rod, which could also be read as five, twenty three, thirty two or one hundred twenty two

hold_back: To keep neighbouring places apart; with zongs only 41 is 4 rods and 1 rod, which could also be read as 5, 23, 32 or 122
maths_rules: base 10 places: tens, then ones; zong is an upright rod and heng is a flat rod
41 with zongs only: 4 upright rods for the tens and 1 upright rod for the ones, 5 rods in a row
with no clear gap the 5 rods read as 5, or 2 then 3 = 23, or 3 then 2 = 32, or 1, 2, 2 = 122
with alternating shapes the tens place takes heng, so 41 = 4 heng and 1 zong, with one reading only
video_script.design: One idea: identical rods give no visible break between places. The five rods stay on the board in a row, and the splits are shown as brackets over the same row.
